title: SAAM Towage celebrates the christening of the Petrel in Arica, Chile's first IMO Tier III tugboat
description:
Marked by the ceremonial smashing of a bottle against the hull, SAAM Towage officially christened the SAAM Petrel in Arica.
As one of the maritime industry’s most cherished and deeply rooted traditions, the christening ceremony symbolizes wishes of good fortune, protection, and safe passage for the vessel and her crew.
The SAAM Petrel is the first tugboat in SAAM Towage’s Chilean fleet to achieve IMO Tier III certification, which enforces stringent standards to slash nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions and reinforces the company’s commitment to sustainable operations.
Designed by Robert Allan and built by the Sanmar Shipyards in Turkey, the vessel is part of SAAM Towage’s regional fleet renewal program.
“The christening of the Petrel truly embodies our purpose as a company: driving sustainable global trade that fosters development and well-being for all.
text:
Marked by the ceremonial smashing of a bottle against the hull, SAAM Towage officially christened the SAAM Petrel in Arica. The state-of-the-art tugboat is set to support ship berthing and unberthing maneuvers across the region.

As one of the maritime industry’s most cherished and deeply rooted traditions, the christening ceremony symbolizes wishes of good fortune, protection, and safe passage for the vessel and her crew. The milestone brought together local authorities, port community representatives, and company employees in a warm and traditional setting.

The SAAM Petrel is the first tugboat in SAAM Towage’s Chilean fleet to achieve IMO Tier III certification, which enforces stringent standards to slash nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions and reinforces the company’s commitment to sustainable operations.

Staying true to SAAM’s tradition of naming vessels after the marine life that defines the waters they navigate, the tug is named after the petrel, a seabird native to the local coastline. Designed by Robert Allan and built by the Sanmar Shipyards in Turkey, the vessel is part of SAAM Towage’s regional fleet renewal program.

“The christening of the Petrel truly embodies our purpose as a company: driving sustainable global trade that fosters development and well-being for all. Investing in these capabilities enables us to keep connecting Chile to the world through services that are increasingly efficient, reliable, and environmentally responsible,” said SAAM CEO Hernán Gómez.

Javiera Hevia, Southern Cone Cluster Manager for SAAM Towage, highlighted the significance of the event for both the port and the local team: “Experiencing this tradition in Arica alongside authorities and our people is a great source of pride. The Petrel not only brings cutting-edge technology to swiftly meet customer demands, but it also reflects our crews’ day-to-day commitment to operating under the highest safety standards.”

The ceremony also featured Jenny Muñoz, a dedicated SAAM team member for 25 years, who served as the godmother (sponsor) of the SAAM Petrel, marking this major company milestone.

title: Sustainable Fuels - DHL - United States of America
description:
At DHL, we have expanded our Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) supply network globally.
Alternative marine fuels may lower well-to-wake GHG emissions relative to petroleum-based marine fuels, depending on the production pathway and engine technology.
LNG dominates this transition, followed by methanol, with ammonia and hydrogen fuels still at an early stage of adoption.
Governments are actively supporting the growth of sustainable fuels through blending mandates, incentives, and regulatory frameworks and major energy companies such as Neste are accelerating investments in low-carbon fuels.
These fuels can reduce lifecycle emissions by up to roughly 75% compared to fossil fuels.
text:
SAF is currently the principal drop-in alternative to conventional jet fuel for reducing lifecycle GHG emissions from long-distance air freight without replacing existing aircraft and fuel infrastructure. Hydrogen and battery solutions remain in early stages, making full electrification not yet viable. As a result, SAF serves as the key commercial pathway for decarbonizing aviation.

Certain SAF pathways can deliver lifecycle GHG-emissions reductions of around 80% compared with conventional aviation fuel, although actual performance varies by feedstock, production pathway, and accounting methodology. Despite this potential, supply remains extremely limited, accounting for only a small share of global aviation fuel, highlighting the urgent need to scale production through greater investment and demand.

In 2025, SAF output reached approximately 2.4 billion liters (1.9 million metric tons), nearly double the 1 million metric tons produced in 2024 – yet it still accounts for only around 0.6% of total jet fuel consumption. SAF production growth is expected to decelerate in 2026 due to high price premiums, policy gaps as well as limited market maturity, underscoring the continued gap between supply and demand.

Availability and high cost remain barriers to widespread adoption. SAFs are derived from renewable sources such as biomass, animal fats, oils, and alcohol, which can be blended with conventional kerosene. Industry initiatives have brought together aviation stakeholders to support SAF market development and the reduction of lifecycle GHG emissions from aviation.

At DHL, we have expanded our Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) supply network globally. By 2025, we used approximately 185 metric kilotons of SAF, achieving a SAF blend of roughly 10% across our air operations. This represents one of the highest SAF utilization shares among global airlines, reflecting DHL's commitment to accelerating the transition toward more sustainable air transport. In May 2026, we added the first SAF production facility in the Middle East to our global network, signing an agreement with SAF One to secure 25,000 metric tons annually for 10 years from the company’s Bahrain plant.

Looking further ahead, hydrogen-derived e-fuels and other synthetic aviation fuels remain promising long-term solutions. Startups like H2FLY and ZeroAvia are working on promising concepts, but experts do not expect commercial application of sub-regional and regional hydrogen fuel cell aircraft before 2030. However, DHL experts view the scaling of SAF from advanced feedstocks such as novel vegetable oils, agricultural residues, and municipal solid waste as the more immediate priority.

International maritime transportation, including vessels ranging from small recreational boats to massive, ocean-going container ships, accounts for roughly 2 to 3% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, with total emissions estimated at 900 to 1,000 million metric tons of CO₂e annually.

More than 80% of global traded goods are transported by cargo ships, 95% of which rely on heavy fuel oil (HFO) for propulsion, a residual fuel produced from petroleum refining, which emits relatively large amounts of GHG when combusted.

Alternative marine fuels may lower well-to-wake GHG emissions relative to petroleum-based marine fuels, depending on the production pathway and engine technology. Some alternatives can also reduce sulfur oxides and certain local air pollutants at the point of use, although pollutant profiles vary by fuel and combustion system.

A wide range of SMFs are being explored, each with distinct characteristics.

Fossil LNG is currently the most widely adopted alternative marine fuel, but its well-to-wake GHG performance relative to fuel oil depends on upstream methane emissions and methane slip from the engine; it therefore remains a fossil-based option.

LPG provides reduced emissions and benefits from established infrastructure, making it a practical near-term option, however its long-term viability is challenged by its fossil origins and strict safety hazards.

Methanol is a versatile and scalable fuel with simpler handling and growing adoption potential, although supply and cost remain challenges.

Biofuels provide a near-term, drop-in solution compatible with existing engines, though scalability is constrained by feedstock availability and sustainability considerations.

Ammonia contains no carbon and therefore produces no CO₂ at the point of use, but its well-to-wake GHG performance depends on how it is produced and managed; storage, toxicity, nitrous oxide emissions, safety, and infrastructure remain challenges.

Electric propulsion enables highly efficient, low-emission operations for short-range vessels but is limited by battery energy density and operational range.

Hydrogen fuel cells produce no CO₂ at the point of use, although lifecycle GHG emissions depend on hydrogen production and supply. Storage volume, infrastructure, safety, and technology maturity remain barriers to maritime deployment.

Nuclear propulsion offers high energy density and produces no direct combustion-related GHG emissions during operation, but lifecycle impacts, radioactive waste, security, regulatory, safety, and public-acceptance issues remain significant.

Taken together, these tradeoffs indicate that the maritime sector will likely follow a multi-fuel transition pathway depending on vessel types, routes, and infrastructure readiness.

Despite low fuel penetration, fleet transition is accelerating rapidly, reflecting a growing readiness to adopt sustainable fuels. In 2025, ship owners increasingly ordered alternative-fuel-capable vessels across leisure and merchant ships. Vessel fuel capabilities are diversified across LNG, methanol, ammonia, and hydrogen-based fuel. LNG dominates this transition, followed by methanol, with ammonia and hydrogen fuels still at an early stage of adoption.

The GHG intensity of maritime transport varies by vessel efficiency, utilization, route, fuel pathway, and the lifecycle boundary applied.

The future of marine fuels is not a single-fuel shift but a gradual transition to a diversified fuel mix, with retrofitting of existing fleets and scaling of alternative fuel supply as the key enablers of decarbonization.

Although electric vehicles (EVs) are rapidly becoming mainstream for short to medium distance transport, especially in light-duty and urban use, electrification remains challenging for long-haul, heavy-duty transport due to limited range, long charging times, and a shortage of suitable high-capacity truck models. This means the industry continues to rely on combustion engines running on fossil fuels.

Sustainable fuels represent a key near-term solution for decarbonization in road transportation, playing a complementary role to electrification, particularly for segments that are difficult to electrify. Biofuels are currently the most practical option because they can be blended with conventional diesel. The IEA forecasts that the share of biofuels in road transportation will rise from 5% in 2022 to 10% in 2030.

This momentum is reinforced by policy and a strong shift by traditional fuel producers toward biofuels and synthetic fuels. Governments are actively supporting the growth of sustainable fuels through blending mandates, incentives, and regulatory frameworks and major energy companies such as Neste are accelerating investments in low-carbon fuels. The company’s capacity is expected to reach roughly 6.8 million metric tons annually by 2027.

The two primary truck biofuels in use are biodiesel (FAME) and hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO). Biodiesel is derived from vegetable oils or waste fats (for example, recycled fats from the catering industry) and can be blended with conventional diesel (typically up to 7% in many regions such as the EU). HVO is vegetable oil that has been treated with hydrogen, offering similar properties to fossil diesel that allow higher blend levels or even 100% substitution.

E-fuels are another emerging class of sustainable fuels, produced using captured CO₂ and green hydrogen from water split by low-carbon electricity sources including wind and solar. These fuels can reduce lifecycle emissions by up to roughly 75% compared to fossil fuels. Adoption remains limited due to high production costs and early-stage commercialization, with large-scale deployment dependent on further technological and policy support.

Warehouses are among the most energy-intensive building types, with material handling, heating, and hot water accounting for a considerable share of total energy demand. Electrification is the default decarbonization pathway, but it has real limits. Alternative fuels may address some warehouse energy uses that are not readily electrified and may reduce relevant Scope 1 emissions, depending on the fuel pathway. Renewable electricity is an energy source rather than a fuel and primarily affects market- or location-based Scope 2 reporting.

Today, a significant share of material handling equipment (MHE) in modern warehouses, such as forklifts and pallet movers, is already electrified and powered by batteries. Electrified material-handling equipment produces no direct exhaust emissions at the point of use; associated Scope 2 and lifecycle GHG emissions depend on the electricity supply and accounting method.

However, battery-powered systems still present operational challenges in high-throughput environments, including charging downtime, battery swapping requirements, and space constraints for charging infrastructure.

Hydrogen fuel cell technology is gaining traction for MHE, particularly in large-scale, high-intensity warehouse operations. Fuel cell-powered forklifts offer continuous operation without battery degradation, significantly reducing downtime. Refueling takes approximately 2 to 3 minutes, compared to several hours required for battery charging, while fuel-cell operation produces no direct CO₂ or combustion-related air-pollutant emissions at the point of use, while lifecycle GHG emissions depend on hydrogen production and supply.

This makes hydrogen particularly suitable for multi-shift, high-utilization environments where operational efficiency and uptime are critical. Leading companies such as Amazon and BMW have already deployed hydrogen fuel cell forklifts at scale in their distribution and manufacturing facilities.

Beyond material handling, building heating and hot water present a different decarbonization hurdle. Electrification of these thermal loads can be challenging at scale, particularly in colder climates or large industrial facilities. In this context, Biomethane upgraded to the applicable gas-grid specification can be used in many existing natural-gas boilers and CHP systems. Its lifecycle GHG performance depends on feedstock, methane leakage, processing, transport, avoided-emissions assumptions, and the accounting method applied.

RNG is chemically identical to fossil natural gas and can be used directly in existing infrastructure, including boilers and combined heat and power (CHP) systems, without requiring major retrofits. Produced from organic waste streams such as agricultural residues, landfill gas, and wastewater, RNG supports circular economy principles while enabling immediate emissions reduction in heating applications.

Sustainable fuels for warehouse operations allow logistics providers to take a more holistic approach to decarbonizing supply chains – extending efforts beyond transport. This supports compliance with emerging regulatory frameworks and aligns with growing customer demand for end-to-end low-carbon logistics solutions.

name: Shipping Industry
title: Ethanol identified as a potential marine fuel | Agri-Pulse Communications, Inc.
description:
The report, Evaluation of Ethanol Use in Marine Shipping, examines ethanol's potential as a lower-carbon fuel for marine vessels, as well as its compatibility with existing methanol-fueled marine engines.
The report estimates the near-term market potential at 2 billion gallons of ethanol annually "under high-substitution scenarios," just looking at the current operating fleet of 112 methanol dual-fuel ships.
Researchers also compared the molecular similarity between methanol and ethanol with no changes in operating a large dual-fuel methanol engine.
The report also says an ethanol spill would have a lower environmental impact than conventional marine fuel.
Ryan LeGrand, U.S. Grains and BioProducts Council president and CEO, said in the same release that expanding marine fuel use could create additional demand for ethanol while providing another market for U.S. corn growers.
text:
Ethanol may offer several advantages for ocean-going vessels, including lower emissions, lower toxicity, existing production capacity and greater energy density than methanol, according to a new report from the National Lab of the Rockies.

The report, Evaluation of Ethanol Use in Marine Shipping, examines ethanol's potential as a lower-carbon fuel for marine vessels, as well as its compatibility with existing methanol-fueled marine engines. The report estimates the near-term market potential at 2 billion gallons of ethanol annually "under high-substitution scenarios," just looking at the current operating fleet of 112 methanol dual-fuel ships.

name: Biofuels & Shipping
title: Biodiesel for shipping has become cheaper than fossil fuels: will this 'green' the industry?
description:
At the same time, the price of environmentally friendly biodiesel has fallen to a record low, which may help accelerate the industry’s transition to a ‘green’ alternative.
Taking into account the costs of implementing the European Union’s climate policies and purchasing emissions allowances, biodiesel has proved to be cheaper than virtually all conventional fuels.
Analysts believe that such an unexpected price imbalance could encourage the shipping industry to switch to more environmentally friendly alternatives.
How to use Biodiesel can be used as fuel for most modern vessels — either on its own or blended with conventional fuel.
Organic waste and agricultural residues are used to produce environmentally friendly fuel.
text:
Due to the war in the Middle East, the price of ‘conventional’ marine diesel fuel continues to rise. At the same time, the price of environmentally friendly biodiesel has fallen to a record low, which may help accelerate the industry’s transition to a ‘green’ alternative.

This was reported by the Financial Times.

In Rotterdam, home to the world’s biodiesel production hub, the price fell to a record low of $985 per metric tonne in September. By way of comparison, as recently as July it was priced at $1,388. According to Argus, producers are cutting prices not only to boost sales, but also to help the EU meet its emissions targets.

Following a record slump, the price has recovered slightly to $1,240 per tonne. Meanwhile, the price of diesel has reached $1,528.5 per tonne. Even before the war in Iran began, a tonne of this fuel cost $714.5.

Taking into account the costs of implementing the European Union’s climate policies and purchasing emissions allowances, biodiesel has proved to be cheaper than virtually all conventional fuels.

Analysts believe that such an unexpected price imbalance could encourage the shipping industry to switch to more environmentally friendly alternatives. Regulatory pressure to reduce emissions provides a further incentive, as shipping accounts for 3 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions.

How to use

Biodiesel can be used as fuel for most modern vessels — either on its own or blended with conventional fuel. However, this requires a few minor modifications. These include, for example, separating the fuel tanks for different types of fuel or adjusting on-board procedures. But these are not particularly complicated or expensive.

Organic waste and agricultural residues are used to produce environmentally friendly fuel. However, biodiesel has a slightly lower energy density. As a result, ships will consume 7–10 per cent more fuel per voyage.

Overall, biodiesel has a significant advantage over other alternatives when it comes to integration into modern shipping. Experts describe it as a ‘practically ready-made solution’.

At the same time, the share of ‘green’ marine fuel worldwide remains negligible — around 0.6 per cent. This is despite an increase in usage since 2021.

Experts attribute this to competition for biofuels with other sectors, such as aviation. At the same time, there are EU restrictions on raw materials, as the EU is wary of crops being diverted from the food sector to the energy sector.

However, according to Argus estimates, demand for high-quality, unblended biodiesel in Rotterdam could rise to 250,000 tonnes this year. Global production stands at just over 4 million tonnes, although biodiesel is more commonly used in other sectors.

text:
The 12th session of IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers (CCC 12) took place last week, progressing work on alternative fuels, onboard carbon capture, cargo safety, dangerous goods and cargo securing.

IMO CCC 12 has drawn attention to the safety gap concerning SP188, which provides exemptions for certain small lithium and sodium batteries.

Tom Bebbington, Industry Engagement & Strategic Partnerships Lead at Tigris, shared some comments on this news:

“We highlighted these issues in our report ‘Before the Fire: Dangerous goods safety and the visibility gap’, says Tom Bebbington, Industry Engagement & Strategic Partnerships Lead’ at Tigris. “The changing shape of goods being moved around the world reflects the global evolution of technologies: for example, the growth of batteries in transit. Such rapid growth has exposed the lack of rigour in the global shipping process and specific issues with Special Provision 188 (SP188), a regulation rule under international transport codes and one of the key regulations governing how lithium cells and batteries move through the supply chain.

“However, there is the risk that we over-rely on data as the solution, particularly when there is a lack of incentive to course-correct. Technology must be designed around human error and human self-interest.

“Data only helps if people are empowered and willing to act on it in time. Even where the risk is visible, fixing it means diverting the vessel, restowing hundreds of containers, delaying the schedule, and burning more fuel.

title: Turkey's Sea of Marmara Ferry Network Could Cut Emissions 63% With Electric Vessels
description:
Turkey’s Sea of Marmara ferry network could cut greenhouse gas emissions by 63% by 2050 by switching to a mix of hybrid and fully electric vessels, an IMO study found.
The study assessed 67 Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax ferries operating across 26 ports, it said in a press release on Tuesday.
A fully electric fleet could cut emissions by 84%, while the reduction could reach 95% if Turkey’s power grid decarbonises in line with its 2053 net-zero target.
The study found that both battery-electric and hybrid propulsion are technically feasible across the ferry operations assessed.
A mix of the two was identified as the most suitable option when balancing emissions cuts and costs.
text:
Turkey’s Sea of Marmara ferry network could cut greenhouse gas emissions by 63% by 2050 by switching to a mix of hybrid and fully electric vessels, an IMO study found.

The study assessed 67 Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax ferries operating across 26 ports, it said in a press release on Tuesday.

The network carries around 25 million passengers and seven million vehicles each year.

A fully electric fleet could cut emissions by 84%, while the reduction could reach 95% if Turkey’s power grid decarbonises in line with its 2053 net-zero target.

The study found that both battery-electric and hybrid propulsion are technically feasible across the ferry operations assessed. A mix of the two was identified as the most suitable option when balancing emissions cuts and costs.

The study found no major technical barriers to electrification, but said charging infrastructure, investment, grid connections and regulatory changes would be needed.

title: NYK shares experience from ammonia-fuelled vessel “Sakigake” at IMO CCC 12
description:
Japanese shipping firm NYK Line on Friday (25 September) said it shared the NYK Group’s initiatives toward the practical deployment of ammonia-fueled vessels during the 12th session of the IMO Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers (CCC 12).
The session was held at the headquarters of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) in London from September 14 to 18.
During the session, NYK shared insights from operating Sakigake, the world’s first commercially operated ammonia-fuelled tugboat, which has accumulated two years of operational experience using ammonia fuel since its delivery in August 2024.
The ceremony provided an opportunity to introduce the NYK Group’s initiatives related to ammonia-fuelled vessels development and its efforts toward decarbonising international shipping to representatives of member states, international organizations, and maritime industry stakeholders.

text:
Japanese shipping firm NYK Line on Friday (25 September) said it shared the NYK Group’s initiatives toward the practical deployment of ammonia-fueled vessels during the 12th session of the IMO Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers (CCC 12).

The session was held at the headquarters of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) in London from September 14 to 18.

During the session, NYK shared insights from operating Sakigake, the world’s first commercially operated ammonia-fuelled tugboat, which has accumulated two years of operational experience using ammonia fuel since its delivery in August 2024.

The company also provided an update on the development of an ammonia-fuelled medium gas carrier (AFMGC) scheduled for delivery in November this year, and shared the Group’s safety philosophy for ammonia-fueled vessels.

On 14 September, NYK donated a model ship of Sakigake to the IMO. During the presentation ceremony, NYK Managing Executive Officer Carl-Johan Hagman presented the model ship to IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez.

The ceremony provided an opportunity to introduce the NYK Group’s initiatives related to ammonia-fuelled vessels development and its efforts toward decarbonising international shipping to representatives of member states, international organizations, and maritime industry stakeholders.

On 17 September, Jun Kato, general manager of NYK’s Engineering Development Group, spoke at the IMO-hosted “Technical Seminar on the Use of Ammonia as Marine Fuel.”

Kato introduced the background to the development of two ammonia-fuelled vessels that NYK has been pursuing since 2021 as part of a Green Innovation Fund Project under Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO).

The seminar also featured presentations by a Master and Chief Engineer from Shin-Nippon Kaiyosha, the operator of Sakigake. Drawing on two years of practical experience operating an ammonia-fuelled tugboat, they shared observations on vessel safety, operational practices, and challenges associated with ammonia-fuelled vessel operations.

The NYK Group will continue to apply the knowledge accumulated through safety management, technological development, and the operation of Sakigake to the development and operation of oceangoing ammonia-fueled vessels.

By leveraging these experiences, the NYK Group aims to promote the practical deployment and wider adoption of ammonia-fuelled vessels, contribute to the establishment of a sustainable ammonia value chain, and support the realization of carbon neutrality in international shipping.

title: Maersk performs in Houston the first supply of 100% bioethanol to a container ship in the US
description:
Maersk has completed in Houston the first commercial operation of ship-to-ship supply of 100% ethanol to an oceangoing container ship in the United States.
POET has supplied the bioethanol from plant sources, while Kirby Corporation has been responsible for the transportation of the fuel and support for the maritime supply operation.
For Maersk, the test allows obtaining information under commercial conditions regarding aspects related to fuel operations, supply infrastructures, sourcing, and logistics chain organization.
The trial with the Tangier Maersk is part of a program previously initiated by Maersk on board the Laura Maersk.
Besides methanol and ethanol, Maersk is working with other options to reduce emissions from its maritime operations.
text:
Maersk has completed in Houston the first commercial operation of ship-to-ship supply of 100% ethanol to an oceangoing container ship in the United States. The fuel, produced from US corn, has been supplied by POET as part of the program with which the Danish shipping company analyzes the incorporation of different fuels into its dual-fuel engine fleet.

The supply has been made to the Tangier Maersk, a 9,000 TEU container ship incorporated this year into the company's fleet and equipped with a dual-fuel propulsion system ready to use methanol. The trial is supported by the existing similarities between methanol and ethanol, both alcohols, which allows studying the use of the latter in systems initially designed for the use of methanol as an alternative fuel.

The operation has involved the participation of various US companies and agencies. POET has supplied the bioethanol from plant sources, while Kirby Corporation has been responsible for the transportation of the fuel and support for the maritime supply operation. The Port of Houston has provided port coordination and the necessary infrastructure, and the US Coast Guard has intervened in the regulatory requirements associated with the procedure.

For Maersk, the test allows obtaining information under commercial conditions regarding aspects related to fuel operations, supply infrastructures, sourcing, and logistics chain organization. The company considers that the development of this alternative will also depend on factors such as product availability, the regulatory framework, and the readiness of various agents in the maritime chain.

“Bioethanol has the potential to contribute meaningfully to the future energy mix for shipping,” said Emma Mazhari, Vice President of Energy Markets at Maersk. According to the company's official, bioethanol may constitute another low-emission fuel option capable of achieving a larger scale and providing more flexibility to the maritime industry in the process of reducing its carbon footprint.

POET, based in South Dakota, produces over 3 billion gallons of bioethanol per year through a network of 35 bioprocessing facilities. The company believes that existing production in the United States, along with the storage, transportation, and distribution networks already developed for this fuel, can facilitate its entry into the maritime market.

The United States is the world's largest producer of ethanol, followed by Brazil, and both countries account for around 80% of global production. The availability of a developed industry is one of the elements that Maersk is analyzing when studying this alternative for its fleet, along with the technical compatibility with vessels prepared to consume alcohol-based fuels.

Jeff Broin, founder and CEO of POET, has linked the Houston operation with the possibility of connecting US agricultural production with the demand for maritime transport fuels. The company believes that the trial allows transporting bioethanol from a market historically linked to land transport towards larger-scale maritime applications.

The trial with the Tangier Maersk is part of a program previously initiated by Maersk on board the Laura Maersk. During a first phase conducted in 2025, the shipping company used a mixture consisting of 10% ethanol and 90% e-methanol to check its integration into the fuel system and analyze aspects such as ignition, combustion, lubricity, corrosion, and emissions.

After that first test, Maersk subsequently raised the ethanol proportion to a mixture of 50% with methanol and continued its trials with higher concentrations. The program has also included operations with the Antonia Maersk, within the analysis that the company conducts on the possibility of using different alcohols in its dual-fuel fleet.

The Tangier Maersk belongs to a new series of medium-sized container ships ordered by Maersk with a nominal capacity of about 9,000 TEU and dual-fuel systems prepared for methanol. Its incorporation expands the number of vessels in the shipping company capable of operating with alternative fuels in addition to conventional marine fuels.

The company maintains a strategy based on studying different energy solutions instead of relying on a single fuel. Besides methanol and ethanol, Maersk is working with other options to reduce emissions from its maritime operations. In the case of bioethanol, the tests developed so far seek to determine its technical behavior on board and the necessary conditions to have supply chains capable of meeting its potential commercial use in different ports.

text:
The shipping industry is at greater risk than ever of missing its 2030 zero-emission fuel targets, according to a new report.

The latest edition of the ‘Climate action in shipping: Progress towards shipping’s 2030 breakthrough’ report tracks the sector’s advancement towards its climate target of having at least 5-10% of the fuel used in international shipping come from scalable zero-emission sources (SZEF) by 2030. This is the estimated uptake needed to meet the ambitions laid out in the 2023 International Maritime Organization (IMO) Greenhouse Gas Strategy, and ultimately, the industry’s entire 2050 net-zero goal.

The report reveals mixed progress towards that swiftly approaching target, with multiple indicators demonstrating the flow-on effects of economic and political upheaval, the crisis in Hormuz, energy security and supply chain concerns, and the regulatory uncertainty caused by the failure to adopt the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework last year.

It tracks progress across five key ‘levers’:

Technology and fuel supply: partially on track

Demand: not on track

Finance: not on track

Policy: not on track

Civil society: partially on track

“The 2030 breakthrough target was embraced by an industry that needs to start bringing tomorrow’s zero-emission fuels to market today if it is going to do its part,” said Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum. “With the right policy push, accelerated industry action can still deliver on this crucial ambition. Adoption of the Net-Zero Framework at the IMO would allow that acceleration to begin in earnest.”

title: The Daily View: Hard NOx truths — why shipping's emissions rules are falling short
description:
Yet regulatory loopholes, limited emissions monitoring and flawed assumptions about vessel operations have left ships emitting far more NOx than regulators intended.
Ships can comply with the letter of the rules while falling a long way short of the environmental outcomes that regulators intended.
More realistic assumptions about vessel operations, combined with continuous emissions monitoring, would provide the data needed to close loopholes and improve air quality.
Shipping faces similar questions over methane slip, nitrous oxide emissions from ammonia engines and the wider decarbonisation agenda.
If a decade of NOx regulation has delivered less than promised, it should serve as a warning for the International Maritime Organization.
text:
TEN YEARS after the IMO’s flagship controls on nitrogen oxide emissions came into force, pollution levels in some of the world’s most environmentally sensitive waters have not fallen in any meaningful way. They may even have worsened.

That uncomfortable reality, highlighted by growing scrutiny of the IMO’s Tier III NOx regime, is about more than air pollution. It exposes a broader weakness in shipping’s environmental rulebook: the gap between regulatory ambition and real-world outcomes.

The NOx story is not one of technological failure. Selective catalytic reduction systems are proven to work, and shipowners have spent billions installing them. Yet regulatory loopholes, limited emissions monitoring and flawed assumptions about vessel operations have left ships emitting far more NOx than regulators intended.

The result is a regime that appears robust on paper but delivers far less environmental benefit in practice. The NOx story exposes a recurring weakness in maritime regulation: success is often measured by compliance rather than performance.

Ships can comply with the letter of the rules while falling a long way short of the environmental outcomes that regulators intended. Installing technology is not the same as ensuring it is used effectively.

Why does that matter? Because commercial realities shape environmental outcomes. Additional monitoring, reporting and maintenance create costs and operational burdens. Unless regulation requires action, operators have little incentive to go beyond minimum compliance.

Fixing the problem is not especially complicated. More realistic assumptions about vessel operations, combined with continuous emissions monitoring, would provide the data needed to close loopholes and improve air quality. The challenge is that tighter oversight raises costs and inevitably faces resistance.

The implications extend far beyond NOx. Shipping faces similar questions over methane slip, nitrous oxide emissions from ammonia engines and the wider decarbonisation agenda. Across all three debates, the challenge is the same: translating regulatory ambition into measurable environmental gains.

If a decade of NOx regulation has delivered less than promised, it should serve as a warning for the International Maritime Organization. Shipping does not lack targets, regulations or technology pathways. What matters is whether they work in practice. Setting ambitious goals is only the start. Measuring performance, closing loopholes and correcting shortcomings may prove just as important as the targets themselves.

Declan Bush

Senior reporter, Lloyd’s List

text:
NYK donated a model of Sakigake to the IMO during the session. Image Credit: NYK

Japan’s shipping firm NYK Line has shared operational experience from its ammonia-fuelled tugboat Sakigake with the IMO.

The company presented its experience during the 12th session of the IMO Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers, held in London from September 14-18, it said in a press release on Friday.

Sakigake, operated by Shin-Nippon Kaiyosha, has accumulated two years of commercial operating experience using ammonia since its delivery in August 2024.

At an IMO technical seminar on September 17, NYK also outlined the safety philosophy and crew-training programmes developed for ammonia-fuelled vessel operations.

The company shared operational knowledge gained from Sakigake, including observations on vessel safety, operating practices and challenges associated with ammonia as a marine fuel.

NYK also provided an update on an ammonia-fuelled medium gas carrier, which is scheduled for delivery in November.

The company said the experience gained from Sakigake would be applied to the development and operation of future oceangoing ammonia-fuelled vessels.

text:
The Comeback: How Canada’s Forests Can Fuel the High Seas

When the Pittsburgh Penguins lowered Mario Lemieux’s iconic Number 66 from the rafters on a cold December night in 2000, it was not merely an athletic resurrection, but a masterclass in the quiet economics of unannounced capability. Lemieux had survived Hodgkin’s lymphoma, endured years of crippling spinal agony, and spent forty-four months in retirement while his plaque cured in the Hockey Hall of Fame; yet thirty-three seconds into his first shift back, he orchestrated a goal that reminded the sports world that true industrial-grade talent does not require a press release—it simply reclaims its place on the ice.

Thousands of miles northwest, across the vast, undulating Boreal expanse of British Columbia and Quebec, Canada’s timber economy finds itself standing in a remarkably similar tunnel, contemplating its own jersey hanging in the rafters of global commerce. For over a century, the vast timberlands that once furnished the masts, spars, hulls, and barrels of the nineteenth-century Atlantic fleet have been relegated to the sidelines by the cheap, dense triumph of petroleum, watching as steel and heavy fuel oil rewrote the laws of maritime navigation. But as the International Maritime Organization’s decarbonization mandates force global shipping to confront the sheer, brutal cost of synthetic fuels, Canada’s timber sector is discovering that its best days were not buried alongside the wooden clipper ship—provided it remembers how to play the game on its own terms.

Long before petroleum tankers or container ships defined the modern horizon, Captain Henry Ward Collier and his contemporaries sailed ships like the Elizabeth Starbuck around a world constructed almost entirely out of forest products. In that era, a merchant vessel was, in the most literal sense, a forest reorganized by craftsmen and dispatched across an ocean, establishing Nova Scotia as a premier nineteenth-century maritime power and turning the St. Lawrence River into a vital commercial artery. When steel replaced oak and heavy fuel oil replaced canvas, the maritime world that Canada had supplied dissolved into history; yet the underlying resource remained vast and untouched, encompassing 369 million hectares of forest—nearly nine percent of the world’s total woodland and almost a quarter of its boreal canopy.

Today, as the maritime sector confronts a generational energy transition, global shipping lines do not need timber to build their hulls, but they desperately need its carbon matrix to fill their fuel tanks.

The central tragedy of the modern bio-economy has rarely been a lack of catalytic brilliance or chemical ingenuity, but rather a fundamental, geographic refusal to look at a map. In the boardrooms of Houston, London, and Zurich, the prevailing dogma of clean-tech engineering dictates that biomass conversion must emulate the grand, centralized scale of petroleum refining—a vision that manifests as multi-billion-dollar gasification complexes designed to convert thousands of daily tonnes of wood chips into pristine, water-white biomethanol.

Yet when one traces the actual supply chains back to forest hubs like Prince George, British Columbia, the sheer thermodynamic absurdity of this centralized dream reveals itself on the back of an envelope. When a mega-gasifier demands six thousand daily tonnes of green forest residues, fully half of that incoming freight is not energy at all, but plain, unadulterated water, accompanied by thousands of additional tonnes of chemically bound oxygen inherent to the lignocellulosic matrix. To force raw timber into a centralized Gulf Coast gasification loop is to design an industrial system whose primary operational expenditure consists of hauling water and oxygen across continents on diesel trucks, running up against a logistical wall that has quietly bankrupted more bio-based ventures than bad catalysts ever could.

What if, instead of dragging the Canadian forest to a distant, mega-scale conversion plant, the initial processing occurred directly at the forest road? This is the core thesis behind a family of distributed conversion technologies that have quietly matured away from the media hype surrounding hydrogen and drop-in synthetic fuels. Fast pyrolysis takes prepared woody biomass, subjects it to rapid thermal cracking in an oxygen-free reactor, and condenses the resulting vapors into a dense, dark renewable liquid known as fast-pyrolysis bio-oil (FPBO). It is acidic, viscous, and aesthetically unappealing, which makes it the perfect candidate to replace bunker fuel. For over a century, the global shipping fleet has demonstrated a pragmatic willingness to burn the heavy, viscous bottoms of the petroleum refining barrel, proving that two-stroke marine engines do not require molecular champagne—they require massive, affordable quantities of liquid energy. By shifting the goal from making a pristine road fuel to producing a pumpable liquid biocrude near the timber harvest, the core engineering question flips from “how do we haul the forest to the refinery?” to “how close can we bring the first liquid step to the trees?”

Commercial models for this distributed architecture are already operating globally, demonstrating that the necessary technology is ready for deployment rather than stuck in pilot testing. In North America, Ensyn has commercialized its Rapid Thermal Processing (RTP) fluid-bed technology, converting forest and mill residues into renewable liquid fuels at facilities like Port-Cartier, Quebec, while establishing strategic refining alliances with Honeywell UOP to co-process biocrude directly within existing refinery Fluid Catalytic Crackers (FCC).

Across the Atlantic, the Netherlands’ BTG-BTL has scaled its proprietary Rotating Cone Reactor technology at the Empyro plant in Hengelo, using solid biochar and process gas internally to generate the thermal energy required to dry incoming wood feedstocks.

Meanwhile, Australia’s Licella has pioneered hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) through its Cat-HTR™ platform, utilizing hot, pressurized water to process wet biomass directly—a pathway currently standing at the Chuntoh Ghuna facility in Prince George, named by the Lheidli T’enneh First Nation to mean “the forest lives,” where Licella and Quadrise are actively developing bio-intermediates specifically for the low-sulfur marine fuel market.

What the shipping industry requires today is not a delicate, highly tailored molecular champagne engineered to pass the exquisite tolerances of a jet engine, but rather a robust, affordable, low-carbon “green sludge” capable of being swallowed by the massive, forgiving maw of a two-stroke marine diesel. Every step up the refining ladder toward pure, water-white diesel consumes massive quantities of expensive green hydrogen to strip away every last oxygen atom; stopping early at a mildly hydrotreated pyrolysis oil (HPO) preserves the carbon yield while delivering a stable, low-viscosity blendstock. By blending 10% to 30% hydrotreated biocrude directly into standard Very Low Sulfur Fuel Oil (VLSFO), marine operators gain an immediate, low-cost path to IMO carbon compliance without requiring fleet-wide engine retrofits or multi-billion-dollar port hydrogen infrastructure.

Canada does not need to invent every reactor, catalyst, or patent involved in this emerging supply chain to establish an effective industrial strategy. The true competitive advantage lies in Canada’s combination of 369 million hectares of forest, an established pulp and timber infrastructure, accessible rail networks, deep-water Atlantic and Pacific ports, and existing petroleum refining assets. By taking wet, bulky slash, running it through rotary shear pre-milling (such as Forest Concepts’ Crumbler® technology) to maximize thermal surface area, drying it with integrated process waste heat, and converting it locally into liquid biocrude, Canada can construct an end-to-end biomass architecture that bypasses the capital-intensity trap of gasification.

When Mario Lemieux returned to the ice, led Canada to Olympic gold in Salt Lake City, and quietly rescued his franchise from bankruptcy, he demonstrated that enduring capability does not rely on self-aggrandizing rhetoric, but on executing proven skills when the game demands them. Canada’s timber economy stands at a similar crossroads, equipped with the land, the ports, and the conversion chemistry required to supply the next generation of low-carbon marine fuels. The forest never left—it simply waited for the maritime world to realize that its answers were sitting in the woods all along.

text:
New York: Buffalo Biodiesel Inc. (BBD), a recycler of used cooking oil (UCO) and producer of renewable feedstocks for renewable diesel and renewable natural gas (RNG) plants, has received a Part 360 permit from the New York Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) for its Tonawanda processing facility, Access newswire reported.

The company invested nearly $3 million in upgrades at the Tonawanda plant to meet regulatory requirements and secure the permit.

“Now that the Tonawanda site has been fully permitted by the DEC, the company can now resume its multimillion-dollar development of the property and its expansion versus out-of-state development,” BBD President Frank V. Balon said.

He said the company appreciated support from the local community, the Governor’s office, the Erie County Executive’s office and the Town of Tonawanda Supervisor’s office for supporting its plans for environmental stewardship and responsible corporate management.

The permit follows BBD’s renewal of its Part 364 Waste Transporter Permit from the DEC, allowing the company to transport UCO across New York State for processing at its Tonawanda facility.

Founded in 2005 and headquartered in Buffalo, New York, Buffalo Biodiesel serves more than 30,000 restaurants across 15 states. The company operates one of the largest UCO collection networks in the Northeastern United States and is expanding its operations to 25 states from Montreal to Miami.

The company said it collected and recycled approximately 31,900 tonnes of UCO in 2025. Based on New York’s Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act greenhouse gas accounting standards, diverting the material prevented an estimated 7,975 tonnes of methane emissions, equivalent to around 685,850 tonnes of carbon dioxide.

According to the company, the climate impact was roughly equivalent to removing 149,100 passenger vehicles from the road for one year.

text:
WASHINGTON, DC, US — A new report by the National Lab of the Rockies (NLR) shows ethanol’s technical, economic and environmental potential as a viable fuel for ocean-going vessels.

The report, “Evaluation of Ethanol Use in Marine Shipping,” details the advantages of ethanol when used as a fuel for ships. This includes molecular similarity to methanol, lower emissions and lower toxicity. In the event of a spill, rapid dissolution and low accumulation reduce long-term environmental problems compared to conventional oil spills.

The report also identifies marine shipping as a potentially significant market for ethanol producers, estimating that the currently operating methanol dual-fuel fleet alone could consume roughly two billion gallons of ethanol annually under high-substitution scenarios.

"This report makes it clear that the American ethanol industry could have a potentially transformative impact on the maritime sector," said Emily Skor, chief executive officer of Growth Energy, a biofuel trade association. "The things that make ethanol such an attractive option as a fuel for ships are the same things that make it vital as a fuel for light-duty vehicles — lower emissions, cost competitiveness, and scalability. We thank NLR for its critical work outlining the ways in which ethanol can meet the needs of today’s shipping sector and look forward to working with our members and the entire industry to secure ethanol's global future as a maritime fuel."

NLR Senior Research Fellow and author of the report Robert McCormick said ethanol is uniquely suited to help the shipping sector achieve its goals.

“We hope this research paves the way for greater collaboration between ethanol producers and shippers, and that it encourages further study to fully grasp the impact ethanol could have in maritime applications,” he said.

US Grains & BioProducts Council (USGBC) President and CEO Ryan LeGrand said the marine fuel market is key to new growth for ethanol.

“Even modest adoption could create billions of gallons of new demand, providing another long-term market for corn growers while helping the shipping industry reduce emissions,” he said.

text:
ATHENS – Brussels should realise that no decision on European shipping can be taken without Greece’s consent, Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said on Monday, as negotiations over a global shipping emissions deal gather pace once again.

Speaking at Posidonia, the biennial global shipping exhibition, Mitsotakis reminded EU partners that the Greek-owned fleet now comprises more than 5,800 vessels, accounting for around 20% of global tonnage and more than 60% of European tonnage.

“It is worth reminding ourselves of this, because it is clear that, when it comes to European shipping, nothing can be done for us without us,” he said.

The Greek premier’s remarks come against the backdrop of intense negotiations over the International Maritime Organisation’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework (NZF), which would cut emissions to 40% below 2008 levels by the end of the decade, and put the sector on a path towards net zero by mid-century.

Global dispute

Last October, major maritime powers clashed over which fuels should qualify as transitional under the new framework.

One camp, led by the United States and Saudi Arabia, argued that liquefied natural gas (LNG) should remain part of the fuel mix, while the EU – largely driven by Denmark – and China favoured new low-carbon fuels such as ammonia and hydrogen.

Following months of deadlock, and with the US threatening sanctions, the negotiating parties were forced to postpone the talks by one year to allow countries to find common ground. Unlike most other EU member states, which had opposed Washington’s move, Greece abstained in the vote. China, meanwhile, sided with the United States at the last minute.

President Donald Trump has praised Greece for its “courage” in abstaining, while Denmark – home to shipping giant Maersk – failed to secure re-election to the IMO Council, of which it had been a member since 2001.

Back to reality

Mitsotakis argued that any agreement reached at the IMO must follow a financially credible and pragmatic pathway towards decarbonisation. LNG should continue to serve as a reliable transitional fuel for global shipping, he said.

Greece’s leading position in global shipping “cannot be sacrificed on the altar of excessive green ambition”, the centre-right prime minister asserted.

Greek shipowners argue that they have invested billions of euros in LNG-powered vessels after natural gas was recognised under the European Green Deal as a ‘transitional’ fuel. Reversing course only a few years later, they say, would undermine the sector’s competitiveness.

“Without realism, there can be no sustainable green transition,” said Melina Travlou, president of the Union of Greek Shipowners.

Travlou stressed that shipping’s decarbonisation depends on factors beyond the sector’s control. “The availability of safe fuels, fit-for-purpose technologies and adequate infrastructure depends entirely on other sectors,” she said.

With time running short ahead of another round of IMO talks in December, EU countries have adopted a new negotiating mandate, signalling that the bloc remains committed to the Net-Zero Framework while being open to adjustments.

“The EU now has a new negotiating mandate aimed at securing fair and pragmatic solutions that will lead to consensus,” EU Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas said, adding that the sector’s competitiveness must remain a priority.

However, Tzitzikostas – another Greek, who hails from the same New Democracy party as Mitsotakis – argued that regulation alone will not deliver the transition. Success, he said, would require close cooperation between governments, ports, shipowners and fuel suppliers, as well as the availability of clean fuels.

‘Not from scratch’

“We oppose starting from scratch, but support retaining the NZF with the realistic changes needed to reach an agreement,” a Commission source told Euractiv in Athens.

Supporters of the framework also oppose reopening negotiations.

The Clean Shipping Coalition, an interest group, has called on governments to resist pressure from what it describes as “petro-states” seeking to derail the framework and instead back the agreement in its current form.

At the last IMO meeting in April, the United States stepped back from its earlier bullying tactics, although it continued to push for a less ambitious outcome.

“Supportive governments will need to remain vigilant and strong in order to parry inevitable future attacks and attempts to further delay adoption,” said John Maggs, the coalition’s IMO representative.

Meanwhile, countries such as Panama and Liberia, the world’s largest flag states, reject the NZF in its current form and are pushing for a fresh deal.

The ETS question

One unresolved issue is the relationship between the NZF and the EU’s Emissions Trading System (ETS), under which shipping companies must purchase allowances for their CO2 emissions.

Shipowners fear they could face two parallel carbon-pricing regimes. While the EU supports the NZF, Brussels has given no indication that it intends to exempt shipping from the cap-and-trade scheme if a global deal enters into force.

The issue could expose divisions within the Commission. Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra and the Directorate-General he heads, DG CLIMA, remain strong supporters of the ETS. Tzitzikostas, however, insisted that companies cannot be expected to pay twice.

“Everyone must understand this, from north to south and from west to east across the European Union,” he said.

The Greek commissioner added that revenues generated through the ETS should be channelled back into the sector to help finance the development and uptake of clean fuels.

text:
Context: The foundation stone for India’s first port-based e-methanol facility was laid at Deendayal Port, Kandla, Gujarat.

The ₹2,300 crore project will produce 150 tonnes daily to fuel international cargo vessels along the Asia–Europe trade corridor.

About India’s First Port-Based e-Methanol Production Facility:

What it is?

A state-of-the-art port-integrated industrial plant designed to produce synthetic, carbon-neutral e-methanol (green methanol) by synthesising green hydrogen generated from renewable electricity with captured biogenic carbon dioxide (CO2).

Organisation: Developed as a joint venture between the Deendayal Port Authority (DPA) under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW) and Namrup-based state PSU Assam Petro-Chemicals Ltd. (APCL), structured under a 76:24 capital contribution ratio.

Located in: Kandla, Gandhidham, Kutch district, Gujarat, sited across 75 acres of port land directly within the logistics zone of the Deendayal Port.

Aim: To decarbonise the maritime shipping sector, transform India into a leading exporter of low-carbon green bunker fuels along the critical Singapore–Rotterdam maritime lane, and accelerate progress toward India’s Net Zero emissions target by 2070.

Key Features:

150 TPD Phased Scalable Modular Capacity: Executed in two phases: Phase I injects ₹1,200 crore to establish 50 tonnes per day (TPD) capacity by January 2027, followed by Phase II adding 100 TPD at ₹1,100 crore by March 2027.

Green Feedstock & Circular Inputs: Relies on dedicated renewable power, on-site desalinated water for green hydrogen electrolysis, and captured biogenic CO2 emissions to produce drop-in marine fuel.

Cost Competitiveness: Engineered to produce green methanol at a benchmark production cost of US$750 per tonne, substantially undercutting current international market prices of approximately US$1,300 per tonne.

Direct DPA Equity & Infrastructure Support: The Deendayal Port Authority contributes an equity stake of ₹567.32 crore, 75 acres of land, dedicated desalinated water pipelines, and renewable energy infrastructure.

Large-Scale Employment Generation: Projected to generate over 3,500 direct and indirect jobs, while building an integrated green molecules ecosystem spanning storage, pipeline transport, bunkering infrastructure, and downstream services.

description:
By Suryakanta ଆମେରିକା ରାଷ୍ଟ୍ରପତି ଡୋନାଲ୍ଡ ଟ୍ରମ୍ପ ଜାତିସଂଘ ସାଧାରଣ ପରିଷଦ (UNGA) ରେ ନିଜର ଅଭିଭାଷଣ ସମୟରେ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସାମୁଦ୍ରିକ ସଂଗଠନ (IMO) ର ଏକ ଯୋଜନା ଉପରେ ବର୍ଷିଛନ୍ତି। ବିଶ୍ୱବ୍ୟାପୀ ସିପିଂ ବା ଜାହାଜ ଚଳାଚଳ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରୁ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ଗ୍ୟାସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନ ହ୍ରାସ କରିବାକୁ ପ୍ରସ୍ତୁତ ହୋଇଥିବା ଏହି ଯୋଜନାକୁ ସେ "ପ୍ରଥମ ବିଶ୍ୱସ୍ତରୀୟ କାର୍ବନ ଟ୍ୟାକ୍ସ" ବୋଲି ଅଭିହିତ କରିଛନ୍ତି। ଏହା ସହିତ ତାଙ୍କ ପ୍ରଶାସନ ହସ୍ତକ୍ଷେପ କରି ଏହାକୁ ବନ୍ଦ କରିବାରେ ସଫଳ ହୋଇଥିଲା ବୋଲି ସେ ଦାବି କରିଛନ୍ତି। ଟ୍ରମ୍ପଙ୍କ 'କାର୍ବନ ଟ୍ୟାକ୍ସ' ଦାବି ଟ୍ରମ୍ପ କହିଛନ୍ତି ଯେ, ଗତବର୍ଷ ଏକ ଅପରିଚିତ ଜାତିସଂଘ ସଂସ୍ଥାକୁ ଗୋପନରେ ବିଶ୍ୱର ପ୍ରଥମ କାର୍ବନ ଟ୍ୟାକ୍ସ ଲାଗୁ କରିବାରୁ ରୋକିବା ପାଇଁ ତାଙ୍କ ପ୍ରଶାସନ ହସ୍ତକ୍ଷେପ କରିବାକୁ ବାଧ୍ୟ ହୋଇଥିଲା। ତାଙ୍କ ମତରେ ଏହି ଟିକସ ଲାଗୁ ହୋଇଥିଲେ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂ ଖର୍ଚ୍ଚ ୧୦ ରୁ ୨୦ ପ୍ରତିଶତ କିମ୍ବା ତା'ଠାରୁ ଅଧିକ ବୃଦ୍ଧି ପାଇଥାନ୍ତା। ସେ ସ୍ପଷ୍ଟ କରିଛନ୍ତି ଯେ, "କୌଣସି ବିଶ୍ୱ ସରକାର ନାହିଁ, ଏବଂ ମୁଁ ରାଷ୍ଟ୍ରପତି ଥିବା ପର୍ଯ୍ୟନ୍ତ କୌଣସି ବିଶ୍ୱସ୍ତରୀୟ ଟିକସ ଲାଗୁ ହେବ ନାହିଁ।" ଆଇଏମଓ (IMO) ର ଯୋଜନା କ'ଣ ଥିଲା?
ପ୍ରକୃତରେ ଆଇଏମଓ ର 'ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ ଫ୍ରେମୱାର୍କ' କୁ ଆନୁଷ୍ଠାନିକ ଭାବରେ ଟିକସ ବୋଲି ବର୍ଗୀକୃତ କରାଯାଇନାହିଁ। ଏହାକୁ ଏକ 'ଗ୍ଲୋବାଲ୍ ପ୍ରାଇସିଂ ମେକାନିଜମ୍' କିମ୍ବା 'ଅର୍ଥନୈତିକ ପଦକ୍ଷେପ' ବୋଲି କୁହାଯାଇଛି। ଏହି ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥା ଅଧୀନରେ ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକ ସେମାନଙ୍କ ନିର୍ଗମନ ପ୍ରଦର୍ଶନ ଆଧାରରେ ଦେୟ ପ୍ରଦାନ କରିବେ। ଏହି ଅର୍ଥ ଏକ ପ୍ରସ୍ତାବିତ IMO ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ ପାଣ୍ଠି କୁ ଯିବାର ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥା ଥିଲା। ୨୦୨୫ ଏପ୍ରିଲ୍ ରେ ବିଭିନ୍ନ ଦେଶ ଏହି ଯୋଜନାକୁ ନୀତିଗତ ଭାବେ ସମ୍ମତି ଦେଇଥିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ଆମେରିକାର ବିରୋଧ କାରଣରୁ ଏହା ସ୍ଥଗିତ ହୋଇଯାଇଥିଲା ଏବଂ ଆସନ୍ତା ଡିସେମ୍ବର ମାସରେ ଏହା ଉପରେ ପୁଣିଥରେ ଆଲୋଚନା ଆରମ୍ଭ ହେବ। ନିୟମ ଓ ପରିବେଶ ଉପରେ ପ୍ରଭାବ ଏହି ଯୋଜନାରେ ନିର୍ଦ୍ଧାରିତ ମାତ୍ରାଠାରୁ ଅଧିକ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ଗ୍ୟାସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନ କରୁଥିବା ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକୁ କ୍ଷତିପୂରଣ ଦେବାକୁ ପଡ଼ିବ, ଯେତେବେଳେ କି ଶୂନ୍ୟ ନିର୍ଗମନ ଜ୍ଞାନକୌଶଳ ବ୍ୟବହାର କରୁଥିବା ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକୁ ଆର୍ଥିକ ପୁରସ୍କାର ମିଳିବ। ଏହି ନିୟମଗୁଡ଼ିକ ମୁଖ୍ୟତଃ ୫,୦୦୦ ଗ୍ରସ୍ ଟନ୍ ରୁ ଅଧିକ ଓଜନର ବୃହତ୍ ସାମୁଦ୍ରିକ ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଉପରେ ଲାଗୁ ହେବାର ଥିଲା, ଯାହାକି ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂରେ ମୋଟ କାର୍ବନ ନିର୍ଗମନର ୮୫ ପ୍ରତିଶତ ପାଇଁ ଦାୟୀ। ସୂଚନାଯୋଗ୍ୟ ଯେ, ବିଶ୍ୱବ୍ୟାପୀ ମୋଟ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନର ୨ ପ୍ରତିଶତ କେବଳ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରୁ ଆସିଥାଏ। ତେଣୁ, ୨୦୫୦ ସୁଦ୍ଧା ସିପିଂ ଶିଳ୍ପକୁ 'ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ' ନିର୍ଗମନ ଲକ୍ଷ୍ୟରେ ପହଞ୍ଚାଇବା ପାଇଁ IMO ଏହି ମହତ୍ତ୍ୱାକାଂକ୍ଷୀ ପଦକ୍ଷେପ ଗ୍ରହଣ କରିଥିଲା। About The Author: Suryakanta

ଆମେରିକା ରାଷ୍ଟ୍ରପତି ଡୋନାଲ୍ଡ ଟ୍ରମ୍ପ ଜାତିସଂଘ ସାଧାରଣ ପରିଷଦ (UNGA) ରେ ନିଜର ଅଭିଭାଷଣ ସମୟରେ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସାମୁଦ୍ରିକ ସଂଗଠନ (IMO) ର ଏକ ଯୋଜନା ଉପରେ ବର୍ଷିଛନ୍ତି। ବିଶ୍ୱବ୍ୟାପୀ ସିପିଂ ବା ଜାହାଜ ଚଳାଚଳ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରୁ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ଗ୍ୟାସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନ ହ୍ରାସ କରିବାକୁ ପ୍ରସ୍ତୁତ ହୋଇଥିବା ଏହି ଯୋଜନାକୁ ସେ "ପ୍ରଥମ ବିଶ୍ୱସ୍ତରୀୟ କାର୍ବନ ଟ୍ୟାକ୍ସ" ବୋଲି ଅଭିହିତ କରିଛନ୍ତି। ଏହା ସହିତ ତାଙ୍କ ପ୍ରଶାସନ ହସ୍ତକ୍ଷେପ କରି ଏହାକୁ ବନ୍ଦ କରିବାରେ ସଫଳ ହୋଇଥିଲା ବୋଲି ସେ ଦାବି କରିଛନ୍ତି।

ଟ୍ରମ୍ପଙ୍କ 'କାର୍ବନ ଟ୍ୟାକ୍ସ' ଦାବି

ଟ୍ରମ୍ପ କହିଛନ୍ତି ଯେ, ଗତବର୍ଷ ଏକ ଅପରିଚିତ ଜାତିସଂଘ ସଂସ୍ଥାକୁ ଗୋପନରେ ବିଶ୍ୱର ପ୍ରଥମ କାର୍ବନ ଟ୍ୟାକ୍ସ ଲାଗୁ କରିବାରୁ ରୋକିବା ପାଇଁ ତାଙ୍କ ପ୍ରଶାସନ ହସ୍ତକ୍ଷେପ କରିବାକୁ ବାଧ୍ୟ ହୋଇଥିଲା। ତାଙ୍କ ମତରେ ଏହି ଟିକସ ଲାଗୁ ହୋଇଥିଲେ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂ ଖର୍ଚ୍ଚ ୧୦ ରୁ ୨୦ ପ୍ରତିଶତ କିମ୍ବା ତା'ଠାରୁ ଅଧିକ ବୃଦ୍ଧି ପାଇଥାନ୍ତା। ସେ ସ୍ପଷ୍ଟ କରିଛନ୍ତି ଯେ, "କୌଣସି ବିଶ୍ୱ ସରକାର ନାହିଁ, ଏବଂ ମୁଁ ରାଷ୍ଟ୍ରପତି ଥିବା ପର୍ଯ୍ୟନ୍ତ କୌଣସି ବିଶ୍ୱସ୍ତରୀୟ ଟିକସ ଲାଗୁ ହେବ ନାହିଁ।"

ଆଇଏମଓ (IMO) ର ଯୋଜନା କ'ଣ ଥିଲା?

ପ୍ରକୃତରେ ଆଇଏମଓ ର 'ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ ଫ୍ରେମୱାର୍କ' କୁ ଆନୁଷ୍ଠାନିକ ଭାବରେ ଟିକସ ବୋଲି ବର୍ଗୀକୃତ କରାଯାଇନାହିଁ। ଏହାକୁ ଏକ 'ଗ୍ଲୋବାଲ୍ ପ୍ରାଇସିଂ ମେକାନିଜମ୍' କିମ୍ବା 'ଅର୍ଥନୈତିକ ପଦକ୍ଷେପ' ବୋଲି କୁହାଯାଇଛି। ଏହି ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥା ଅଧୀନରେ ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକ ସେମାନଙ୍କ ନିର୍ଗମନ ପ୍ରଦର୍ଶନ ଆଧାରରେ ଦେୟ ପ୍ରଦାନ କରିବେ। ଏହି ଅର୍ଥ ଏକ ପ୍ରସ୍ତାବିତ IMO ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ ପାଣ୍ଠି କୁ ଯିବାର ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥା ଥିଲା। ୨୦୨୫ ଏପ୍ରିଲ୍ ରେ ବିଭିନ୍ନ ଦେଶ ଏହି ଯୋଜନାକୁ ନୀତିଗତ ଭାବେ ସମ୍ମତି ଦେଇଥିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ଆମେରିକାର ବିରୋଧ କାରଣରୁ ଏହା ସ୍ଥଗିତ ହୋଇଯାଇଥିଲା ଏବଂ ଆସନ୍ତା ଡିସେମ୍ବର ମାସରେ ଏହା ଉପରେ ପୁଣିଥରେ ଆଲୋଚନା ଆରମ୍ଭ ହେବ।

ନିୟମ ଓ ପରିବେଶ ଉପରେ ପ୍ରଭାବ

ଏହି ଯୋଜନାରେ ନିର୍ଦ୍ଧାରିତ ମାତ୍ରାଠାରୁ ଅଧିକ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ଗ୍ୟାସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନ କରୁଥିବା ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକୁ କ୍ଷତିପୂରଣ ଦେବାକୁ ପଡ଼ିବ, ଯେତେବେଳେ କି ଶୂନ୍ୟ ନିର୍ଗମନ ଜ୍ଞାନକୌଶଳ ବ୍ୟବହାର କରୁଥିବା ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକୁ ଆର୍ଥିକ ପୁରସ୍କାର ମିଳିବ। ଏହି ନିୟମଗୁଡ଼ିକ ମୁଖ୍ୟତଃ ୫,୦୦୦ ଗ୍ରସ୍ ଟନ୍ ରୁ ଅଧିକ ଓଜନର ବୃହତ୍ ସାମୁଦ୍ରିକ ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଉପରେ ଲାଗୁ ହେବାର ଥିଲା, ଯାହାକି ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂରେ ମୋଟ କାର୍ବନ ନିର୍ଗମନର ୮୫ ପ୍ରତିଶତ ପାଇଁ ଦାୟୀ। ସୂଚନାଯୋଗ୍ୟ ଯେ, ବିଶ୍ୱବ୍ୟାପୀ ମୋଟ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନର ୨ ପ୍ରତିଶତ କେବଳ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରୁ ଆସିଥାଏ। ତେଣୁ, ୨୦୫୦ ସୁଦ୍ଧା ସିପିଂ ଶିଳ୍ପକୁ 'ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ' ନିର୍ଗମନ ଲକ୍ଷ୍ୟରେ ପହଞ୍ଚାଇବା ପାଇଁ IMO ଏହି ମହତ୍ତ୍ୱାକାଂକ୍ଷୀ ପଦକ୍ଷେପ ଗ୍ରହଣ କରିଥିଲା।

title: TEHA Group and Eni publish strategic study on renewable biofuels for Europe
description:
TEHA Group and Eni have presented a joint strategic study, Sustainable biofuels as a strategic lever for industrial competitiveness, energy security and decarbonisation, at the Cernobbio Forum.
The report argues that biofuels from renewable feedstocks — particularly HVO and SAF — offer an immediately available solution to cut transport emissions while strengthening Europe’s energy security and industrial base.
It warns that replacing one dependency with another in the energy transition could leave Europe exposed to new geopolitical risks, and calls for a more pragmatic, industrially focused policy framework.
Eni highlights its experience converting traditional refineries into biorefineries and deploying HVO across European road transport, demonstrating how innovation and existing skills can drive sustainable transformation.
The study positions biofuels as complementary to electrification, enabling rapid decarbonisation of existing vehicle fleets using current infrastructure, and supporting European competitiveness in advanced fuels technologies.

text:
The IMO’s Research and Development Forum has examined how the growing use of alternative marine fuels could change pollution-response requirements.

Held on September 21-22 in Singapore, the forum brought together regulators, scientists, industry representatives and emergency responders to discuss preparedness for incidents involving newer marine fuels.

Hosted by Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, with support from China, the event covered LNG, LPG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, biofuels and e-fuels.

Discussions focused on how the different properties of these fuels could affect spill behaviour and response strategies.

Participants also looked at spill modelling, risk assessment, emergency response, post-spill actions and international cooperation.

The forum included expert presentations, case studies, panel discussions and working sessions, allowing participants to share research and operational experience.

A key theme was the need for closer cooperation between governments, industry, academia and the scientific community to address knowledge gaps and improve preparedness before major incidents occur.

Participants also stressed the importance of using research findings, operational experience and international cooperation to develop response protocols for alternative fuels.

text:
The shipping industry will likely miss its 2030 targets for vessels running on alternative fuels, according to a new study from the UCL Energy Institute, mainly due to the regulatory uncertainties surrounding the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF).

According to the fifth edition of 'Climate action in shipping: Progress towards shipping's 2030 breakthrough', the industry is highly unlikely to meet targets of having zero-emission fuels accounting for 5-10 percent of total fuel usage, the goal set in the 2023 IMO Greenhouse Gas Strategy. The ultimate goal is to ensure the shipping industry becomes net-zero by 2050, and the 2030 target was conceived as an enabler to accelerate early progress.

The 2030 targets meant that some 600-1,200 large ships with a capacity of at least 15,000 TEU (or equivalent) would be running on scalable zero-emissions fuels (SZEF). However, owing to headwinds like economic and political upheaval, the Strait of Hormuz crisis, energy security and supply chain concerns, and the regulatory uncertainty caused by the failure to adopt the NZF, the world is lagging behind on its alternative fuel goals. In 2025, the milestone of having roughly 100 15,000-TEU-equivalent ships running on SZEF was not met.

The UCL Energy Institute and the Getting to Zero Coalition report shows that while the world is falling behind on its goals, there have been notable achievements across the five key 'levers' being used to assess the industry's progress - namely technology and supply, demand, finance, policy, and civil society.

Supply of alternative fuels and technologies has, for instance, been progressing. The number of ports offering methanol bunkering now stands at 29, up from 19 a year ago. The world has also witnessed sea trials of the first large ammonia-fueled vessels with two-stroke engines being successfully completed, as well as the building of smaller ammonia-fueled supply vessels and tugboats fitted with four-stroke engines. The industry has also recorded its first ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering operation.

The report shows that the long-anticipated wave of methanol-capable container ship deliveries finally landed in 2025, tripling methanol-capable in-service tonnage from 2.3 million to 7.7 million gross tonnage (GT) and pushing the SZEF-capable share of the active fleet from 0.41 percent to 0.77 percent. This was the largest single-year capability gain on record, delivered through 56 newbuilds totaling 5.4 million GT. However, the order book regressed, with SZEF-capable orders falling from 9.5 percent to 5.7 percent of total GT orders.

On finance, the progress has been mixed: issuances of shipping-specific sustainable debt have plateaued. In 2025, approximately $3 billion was issued to shipping-related entities through green loans, green bonds, sustainability-linked loans, and transition instruments, down from $3.4 billion in 2024.

For the industry, the controversies surrounding the NZF have become one of the major roadblocks towards the 2030 goals, with the U.S. being among its staunchest opponents. The report reckons that with the NZF remaining in limbo, the policy clarity required for the 2030 goal is a major obstacle.

“The failure to adopt the NZF was the single most transition-regressive event we've seen in the five years this report has been running,” said Pinar Langer, research fellow at the UCL Energy Institute.

She added that reversing this momentum loss and securing regulatory certainty is one of the most important next steps to give shipowners the confidence to order zero-emission vessels, lenders the incentive to invest in them, and charterers the motivation to pay for low-carbon shipping.

title: IMO targets alternative fuel spill response | Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide
description:
Participants at an International Maritime Organization (IMO) forum have called for greater cooperation to address gaps in spill-response preparedness as shipping expands its use of alternative bunker fuels.
The IMO’s two-day research and development forum, held in Singapore on 21–22 September, examined how the different properties of LNG, LPG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen and biofuels could affect marine pollution incidents and emergency response operations.

text:
The number of B100 samples ENGINE recorded in Rotterdam more than doubled in the first eight months of 2026 from a year earlier, lifting its share of the port’s biofuel samples to almost a quarter.

ENGINE recorded 77 B100 fuel quality samples in Rotterdam between January and August, up 126% from 34 in the same period last year.

In total, ENGINE had data for 342 biofuel samples in Rotterdam between January and August 2026, up from 275 in the same period of 2025.

ENGINE’s sample data covers only part of Rotterdam’s biofuel bunker market. In the first half of 2026, suppliers in the Dutch port sold around 345,000 mt of what the Port of Rotterdam Authority classes as bio-blended fuel oils and distillates.

ENGINE’s samples for the same period cover around 135,000 mt, or 39%, of those sales. Some samples do not have a quantity recorded, so actual coverage is somewhat higher.

The port authority does not report B100 sales as a separate category, so no official B100 figures exist for the port. The number of B100 samples in ENGINE’s data can therefore act as an indicator of how demand for the fuel is trending in Rotterdam.

B100’s share of Rotterdam’s biofuel samples rose to 23% in the first eight months of 2026, from 12% in the same period of 2025.

Most other biofuel grades lost share. B30-VLSFO accounted for 28% of samples, down from 37%. B30-LSMGO’s share slipped from 22% to 20%, and B30-HSFO’s fell from 7% to 3%.

B30-ULSFO was the only other grade to gain share, rising from 22% to 27%.

Rotterdam is currently the largest bunker hub in the world by marine biofuel volumes. The port’s demand is supported by the Netherlands’ implementation of the EU’s RED III directive, which incentivises bunkering of biofuels, making them considerably cheaper in Rotterdam than in other European ports.

Under Dutch rules, bunker suppliers in the country’s ports can generate maritime emission reduction units, known as ZRE A tickets, by selling low-emission marine fuels such as biofuels made from advanced feedstocks listed in the directive, including palm oil mill effluent.

These ZRE A tickets can then be sold to suppliers of conventional fuels such as VLSFO or LSMGO, who need them to meet their own obligations.

The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and FuelEU Maritime add a further pull, as both reward shipowners for burning biofuel with lower carbon costs and smaller compliance penalties.

ENGINE’s samples show 15 bunker suppliers selling biofuels in Rotterdam in the first eight months of 2026, up from 10 in the same period last year. The number selling B100 rose from three to seven.
